items.prompt: Which muscles are the primary movers in a barbell back squat?

options.label: Lats and rhomboids
Quadriceps and glutes
Chest and triceps
Biceps and forearms

rubric: The squat mainly drives the hips and knees, which the glutes and quadriceps extend.
Other options name upper-body muscles used in pulling or pressing.

items.prompt: What is progressive overload?

options.label: Training to complete failure on every set
Switching to new exercises every single session
Gradually increasing the demand placed on the muscles
Repeating the same workout without any changes

rubric: Progressive overload means steadily raising the training stimulus (weight, reps, sets).
Distractors confuse it with constant routine, random variety or maximal effort.

items.prompt: In strength training, what is a 'set'?

options.label: The total weight moved during a workout
A group of consecutive reps done without resting
One single lift and lowering of the weight
The rest period taken between two exercises

rubric: A set is a block of consecutive repetitions.
One lift is a rep; total weight moved is volume load.

items.prompt: Which spine position is recommended during a squat or deadlift?

options.label: Strongly arched backward
Fully rounded forward
Flexed to shorten the lift
Neutral, keeping its natural curves

rubric: A neutral spine spreads load safely.
Rounding or over-arching under load raises injury risk.

items.prompt: Which nutrient is most closely linked to repairing and building muscle tissue?

options.label: Vitamin C
Dietary fibre
Protein
Sodium

rubric: Protein supplies the amino acids used for muscle repair and growth.
The others support health but are not the main building material.

items.prompt: Which of these are compound lifts, meaning they work several joints and muscle groups at once? Select all that apply.

options.label: Leg extension
Barbell back squat
Biceps curl
Bench press
Deadlift

rubric: Squat, deadlift and bench press move multiple joints.
Curls and leg extensions isolate a single joint.

items.prompt: A new gym member reads their program card: 'Bench press 3 x 8 at 40 kg'. They ask a trainer what the notation means. The trainer wants to give the correct reading of it.

options.label: Three sets of eight reps, each with 40 kg
Eight sets of three reps, each with 40 kg
Three sets totalling eight reps at 40 kg
Eight minutes of bench work with 40 kg

rubric: The notation is sets x reps at a given load.
Reversing the order or totalling reps are common misreadings.

items.prompt: Why do beginners often get noticeably stronger in their first weeks, before much muscle has been added?

options.label: Mostly because muscle size doubles within the first fortnight
Mostly because tendons lengthen to give extra leverage
Mostly because the nervous system learns to use muscle better
Mostly because body fat turns directly into muscle fibre

rubric: Early gains come largely from neural adaptation and skill learning.
Muscle growth is slower, and fat does not convert to muscle.

items.prompt: Why is rest between hard sessions for the same muscle group important?

options.label: Muscles adapt and grow during recovery, not during lifting
Muscles grow only while the weight is actively moving
Rest removes the need for sleep and proper food
Rest resets strength to the starting level each week

rubric: Training provides the stimulus; adaptation happens in recovery.
Distractors misplace where growth occurs or misstate rest's effect.

items.prompt: Which example best illustrates progressive overload?

options.label: Swapping every exercise each week to avoid boredom
Dropping the weight to finish more reps by momentum
Adding 2.5 kg once all reps were completed with good form
Using the same weight for months to perfect technique

rubric: Raising load after mastering the current one increases the stimulus.
Other options keep or reduce demand, or change variables randomly.

items.prompt: A lifter does the same weight, sets and reps every session for several months. What is the most likely result?

options.label: Strength keeps rising at the same rate
Progress slows or stalls as the body adapts
Strength drops because muscles forget the load
Muscle grows faster due to the consistency

rubric: Without increased demand, adaptation plateaus.
Consistency alone does not keep driving gains.

items.prompt: Why should a lifter do lighter warm-up sets before heavy work?

options.label: They use up energy so the heavy sets feel easier to skip
They permanently increase the weight a muscle can lift
They raise muscle temperature and rehearse the movement at low risk
They replace the need for good technique on working sets

rubric: Warm-up sets prepare tissues and groove the movement pattern.
They do not substitute for technique or build lasting strength themselves.

items.prompt: Which statements explain why good lifting form matters? Select all that apply.

options.label: It keeps tension on the intended muscles
It makes progress measurable and repeatable
It lowers the chance of injury under load
It lets the same weight feel lighter forever

rubric: Good form targets muscles, protects joints and makes loads comparable.
Form does not permanently reduce how heavy a weight is.

items.prompt: Sam trains four hard days a week but sleeps about five hours a night. Over three weeks Sam feels constantly sore and the usual weights are getting harder, not easier. A friend asks what this most likely means.

options.label: The program is too easy and needs more daily sessions
Soreness proves the workouts are working perfectly
Recovery is inadequate, so adaptation is not keeping up
Muscles are shrinking because of too much protein

rubric: Persistent soreness and falling performance suggest under-recovery from poor sleep.
Adding more sessions or treating soreness as proof of progress ignores recovery.

items.prompt: Why must a lifter gradually increase the training demand over time to keep getting stronger?

options.label: Muscles store up fatigue from each session, so heavier loads are needed to burn off the accumulated tiredness
The nervous system gets bored of familiar exercises, so the weights must change for motivation to stay high
The body adapts to a given stress, so the same workload eventually stops giving a new reason to adapt
Lighter weights train only the tendons, so muscle growth requires a heavier load after the first month

rubric: Adaptation occurs in response to a stress; once adapted, the same stress no longer drives change.
Distractors treat overload as fatigue management or boredom rather than adaptation.

items.prompt: Why is sleep considered part of a strength program rather than just a lifestyle extra?

options.label: Sleep burns stored fat that sits over muscle, which makes the strength gained in training look larger
Sleep resets the weights a lifter can handle, so skipping it lowers the load but doesn't affect growth
Muscles grow during the workout itself, and sleep only restores the energy used for the next session
Most repair and adaptation to training happens during recovery, and poor sleep can blunt those gains

rubric: Adaptation occurs during recovery, not during the lifting itself.
Distractors claim growth occurs in the session or that sleep only affects energy.

items.prompt: Which of these is a compound lift?

options.label: Biceps curl
Lateral raise
Leg extension
Barbell back squat

rubric: A compound lift moves multiple joints and muscle groups; the squat uses hips, knees and ankles.
The others are single-joint isolation exercises.

items.prompt: Why is it advised to keep the barbell close to the body during a deadlift?

options.label: A close bar makes the legs do less work, so the back can rest during the lift
A far bar increases the leverage on the lower back, so the spine takes more strain for the same weight
A close bar shortens the distance the bar travels, so the lifter finishes the rep faster
A far bar causes the grip to open up, so the hands tire before the legs and back do

rubric: Keeping the bar close shortens the lever arm at the hips and lower back, lowering strain.
Distractors invent unrelated effects like leg work, speed or grip.

items.prompt: A lifter wants to build maximal strength. Which general approach fits that goal best?

options.label: Very light loads for 30 or more reps per set, to practise endurance
Moderate loads that can be lifted for 15 to 20 reps with short rests
Bodyweight movements only, done as fast as possible without added load
Heavy loads in roughly the 1 to 5 rep range, with longer rests between sets

rubric: Heavy loads at low reps with longer rests best train maximal force output.
Other options target endurance or ignore load.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly explain why compound lifts are a good base for a beginner's plan? Select all that apply.

options.label: They isolate one muscle so that the others can recover during the session
They build coordination across joints that carries over to other movements
They train several muscle groups in one movement, which saves time
They remove the need for rest days because the load is spread out
They let the lifter use heavier loads than most single-joint exercises

rubric: Compound lifts are time-efficient, allow heavy loading and build multi-joint coordination.
Distractors claim they remove rest needs or isolate muscles, which is false.

items.prompt: Maya finished her first week of squats and lunges. Two days later her legs feel very sore and stiff, and the soreness fades after about four days. She wonders if she injured herself. What is the best interpretation?

options.label: It is likely delayed onset muscle soreness from a new stimulus, and it usually fades without treatment
It shows her muscles grew a lot, so more soreness means better results in every session
It proves she lifted too heavy, so she should stop training legs for at least a month
It signals torn muscle fibres that need complete rest until all stiffness is gone

rubric: Soreness that peaks a day or two after a new stimulus and fades is typical DOMS.
Distractors treat soreness as proof of injury or as a direct measure of growth.

items.prompt: A lifter squatted 100 kg for 3 sets of 5 and completed every rep. Using linear progression with 2.5 kg added each session, what should she lift next session?

options.label: 102.5 kg for 3 sets of 5
105 kg for 3 sets of 5
97.5 kg for 3 sets of 5
100 kg for 3 sets of 8

rubric: Linear progression adds a fixed small amount when all reps were completed: 100 + 2.5 = 102.5 kg.
Distractors misuse the increment or change reps.

items.prompt: Lifting 80% of a 100 kg one-rep max, how heavy is the bar?

options.label: 125 kg
90 kg
80 kg
20 kg

rubric: 80% of 100 kg is 80 kg.
Other values come from wrong percentage arithmetic.

items.prompt: A program calls for dumbbell presses of 3 sets in the 8 to 12 rep range. A lifter does 12, 12, 12 with 20 kg dumbbells. Using double progression, what should come next session?

options.label: Add a fourth set at 20 kg and stay at 12 reps
Move to a heavier dumbbell and work back up from about 8 reps
Drop to 15 kg and try to do 12 reps again on each set
Keep 20 kg and aim for 15 reps on every set

rubric: Double progression raises reps to the top of the range, then raises weight and restarts at the bottom.
Distractors ignore the rep range or lower the load.

items.prompt: Sam wants a three-day full-body plan with a rest day between sessions. Which schedule fits?

options.label: Thursday, Friday, Saturday
Saturday, Sunday, Monday
Monday, Wednesday, Friday
Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday

rubric: Monday, Wednesday, Friday leaves a rest day between full-body sessions.
The others put sessions on consecutive days.

items.prompt: A beginner has failed to complete the target reps on the bench press for three sessions in a row at the same weight. Sleep and food have been normal. What is the most sensible next step?

options.label: Add 5 kg next session to force the body to adapt faster
Stop training bench press permanently and switch to push-ups
Do the same weight again for a month with no change at all
Reduce the weight by about 10% and build back up over the following weeks

rubric: After repeated stalls a reset of about 10% allows recovery and renewed progress.
Distractors add load, quit, or keep repeating the failure.

items.prompt: A lifter will do working sets of squats at 100 kg. Which of these make a sensible warm-up ramp? Select all that apply.

options.label: 120 kg for 1 rep
Empty bar for 8 reps
50 kg for 5 reps
100 kg for 15 reps
75 kg for 3 reps

rubric: A ramp starts light and rises toward the working weight with fewer reps so fatigue stays low.
The 100 kg x 15 tires the lifter, and 120 kg exceeds the working load.

items.prompt: During a set of five deadlifts at 90 kg, Jo notices her lower back starts to round on the fourth and fifth reps. She has two more sets planned at the same weight. What should she do?

options.label: Keep 90 kg and use a lifting belt to hide the rounding in the later reps
Do the remaining sets with fewer warm-ups to save energy for the reps that break down
Lower the weight so that all reps are done with a neutral back, then build up again
Increase to 100 kg so the first reps feel easy and the form holds from fatigue

rubric: Form breakdown means the load or volume is too high for now; reduce it and rebuild with good form.
Distractors cover up the problem or raise the risk.

items.prompt: A lifter squats 100 kg for 5 reps and uses linear progression, adding 2.5 kg every session. If every session succeeds, what is the load on the fourth session?

options.label: 110 kg
105 kg

rubric: Session 1 is 100 kg, so three increments of 2.5 kg give 107.5 kg on session 4.
110 kg counts four increments, a common miscount of the starting session.

items.prompt: A dumbbell row uses a 8-12 rep range for 3 sets. Today the lifter got 12, 12, 12 with 30 kg. Under double progression, what should the next session look like?

options.label: Stay at 30 kg and aim for 15 reps on every set
Add a small amount of load and still demand 12 reps
Drop back to 8 reps per set at the same 30 kg
Add a small amount of load and restart near 8 reps

rubric: Double progression raises reps to the top of the range, then raises load and resets reps to the bottom.
Adding load while demanding the top reps ignores the reset; going past the range abandons the scheme.

items.prompt: Using the Epley formula, 1RM = weight x (1 + reps/30), what is the estimated 1RM for a set of 6 reps with 80 kg?

options.label: 96 kg
104 kg
86 kg
92 kg

rubric: Other values come from mis-scaling the rep term.

items.prompt: A program prescribes sets of 5 at 75% of a 160 kg squat 1RM. Which load should the lifter put on the bar?

options.label: 120 kg
115 kg
125 kg
110 kg

rubric: Other values come from using the wrong percentage or mis-multiplying.

items.prompt: A lifter can train 4 days a week and wants each major muscle group trained twice weekly, with a rest day between sessions that hit the same muscles. Which schedule fits?

options.label: Mon upper, Tue upper, Thu lower, Fri lower
Mon push, Tue pull, Thu legs, Fri rest day only
Mon upper, Tue lower, Thu upper, Fri lower
Mon full body, Tue full body, Wed full body, Thu full body

rubric: Upper/lower alternation hits each region twice a week and spaces the repeats by several days.
The other options hit muscles once or put the same muscles on back-to-back days.

items.prompt: After six hard weeks, a lifter plans a deload week. Which plans correctly apply a deload? Select all that apply.

options.label: Test one-rep maxes on every lift to measure progress
Take a full month off from lifting to ensure recovery
Cut weekly sets by about half and keep technique practice
Keep the same exercises with loads around 60-70% of normal

rubric: A deload cuts volume and/or intensity briefly while keeping the movement pattern.
A month off is detraining, and max testing adds stress instead of reducing it.

items.prompt: A lifter follows a 5x5 bench program at 70 kg and adds load only when every set is completed. Today the sets were 5, 5, 5, 5, 4 reps with good form. The lifter wants to know what to do next session.

options.label: Switch to 3x10 at 70 kg for a new stimulus
Repeat 70 kg and aim to complete all 5x5
Add 2.5 kg because four sets were completed
Drop to 60 kg for a week to rebuild confidence

rubric: The rule is to add load only after all prescribed reps are done, so the load repeats.
Adding anyway breaks the rule; dropping or switching changes the plan without need.

items.prompt: In a back squat, a lifter's hips rise faster than the chest out of the bottom, so the lift turns into a good morning. Which cause best explains it?

options.label: Quads are weak compared with hips and back, shifting load to the hips
Excess upper-back strength is holding the torso too upright
Too little ankle mobility, which always causes hips to rise first
A bar placed slightly high on the traps, which pulls the hips back

rubric: When the quads cannot drive the knees and torso up, the lifter shifts the effort to the hips and back.
The distractors name factors that either do not cause this pattern or would change it differently.

items.prompt: An intermediate lifter's squat has stalled for three weeks. The log shows 5 hours of sleep, a 500 kcal daily deficit, an unchanged program, and bar speed slowing at the same loads. What best explains the stall?

options.label: The lifter needs more sets per session regardless of other factors
Squat technique has regressed, even though the bar speed data show nothing
Recovery capacity is reduced, so the same work can no longer drive adaptation
The muscles have adapted to the program and need more variety

rubric: Poor sleep and an energy deficit reduce recovery, which fits slowing bar speed on an unchanged program.
The other options ignore the recovery evidence in the log.

items.prompt: In a conventional deadlift, the bar drifts away from the shins and the lower back rounds just as the bar passes the knees. The start off the floor looks fine. Which diagnosis best fits?

options.label: The lats are not engaged, so the bar swings forward and lengthens the back's lever arm
The hips started too low, which only affects the first inch off the floor
The grip is too strong, which makes the bar travel in a straight line
The lifter locked out too early, which cannot affect the pull at the knees

rubric: A bar drifting forward increases the moment arm on the lower back, and unengaged lats allow it.
The distractors describe causes that act at other points of the lift or do not produce drift.

items.prompt: Two plans give 9 weekly chest sets. Plan A splits them into 3 sets on each of 3 days. Plan B does all 9 sets on one day. Which comparison best explains why Plan A often works better?

options.label: Plan B cannot be progressed because heavy days are not allowed
Plan A trains the muscle more often, so sets stay higher quality and technique gets more practice
Plan A raises weekly volume, which is why it works better
Plan A has fewer total sets, so it avoids all fatigue

rubric: Equal volume spread across more sessions limits per-session fatigue and increases practice frequency.
Both plans have equal weekly volume, and Plan B can still be progressed.

items.prompt: A lifter reviews the training log. Which patterns point to accumulated fatigue rather than a need for a harder program? Select all that apply.

options.label: Every lift has improved week to week
Poor sleep and achy joints appear along with a performance dip
Usual loads feel heavier for two weeks and bar speed slows
Reps and loads have risen steadily each week
Every set ends with 3+ reps in reserve and mood is good

rubric: Heavier-feeling loads, slower bar speed, poor sleep and achy joints with a performance dip signal fatigue.
Easy sets and steady gains suggest the program is still working or is too easy.

items.prompt: A lifter's bench press keeps rising but the squat has stalled. The week has a heavy deadlift session on Thursday and the heavy squat session on Friday. Squat sets on Friday feel slow and the lower back is tired. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: Bench press gains are drawing recovery away from the legs
Squat form needs no changes, so the stall is purely random
Heavy deadlifts the day before are fatiguing the lower back, which limits squat quality
Squats are being done too often to allow adaptation of the quads

rubric: Both lifts load the lower back and posterior chain, so sequencing heavy pulls the day before degrades the squat.
Bench press does not compete for leg recovery in this way, and a stall with a clear pattern is not random.

items.prompt: A lifter raises weekly chest volume from 10 to 20 sets. After a month, strength has not improved, soreness persists, and workouts feel worse. What is the best interpretation?

options.label: The lifter is probably beyond the volume they can recover from
The soreness shows the muscle is growing faster than before
The stall proves the exercises are no longer effective for chest
The lifter needs even more sets to push through the plateau

rubric: Doubling volume can exceed recoverable volume, producing persistent soreness and no progress.
Persistent soreness with flat strength is not a sign of faster growth, and the exercises are not the cause.

items.prompt: A lifter's back squat stalls. On heavy reps the hips shoot up first out of the bottom, the torso folds forward, and the bar drifts toward the toes. Which diagnosis best explains the whole pattern?

options.label: The quadriceps are weak relative to the hips and back, so the hips take over the lift
The lifter's stance is too narrow, which by itself forces the torso to fold forward
The lifter's grip on the bar is too wide, which pushes the chest down into the hips
The hamstrings are too strong, so they pull the knees backward and shift the bar forward

rubric: Hips rising first with a forward lean is the classic sign of quads lagging behind the posterior chain, so the load shifts to the hips.
Stance and grip distractors name real setup variables but do not explain the sequence of the faults.

items.prompt: An intermediate lifter on a 5x5 program uses the same load for all sets with 90 seconds of rest. Reps fall 5, 5, 4, 3, 3 each session, although the first two sets feel manageable. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The load is far above the lifter's true maximum, so even the first sets should fail
The lifter has plateaued in strength and needs to stop training that lift for months
The lifter's muscles have adapted to five reps, so the rep range must change at once
Rest between sets is too short to restore performance at this load, so later sets suffer

rubric: Strong first sets followed by a steady drop point to incomplete recovery between sets, not a load that is too heavy.
Distractors treat a within-session fatigue pattern as a long-term plateau or as an unsuitable rep range.

items.prompt: A lifter trains upper/lower 4 days a week, and a friend trains full body 3 days a week. Weekly sets per muscle are equal. Which difference between the plans most plausibly matters for the quality of each session?

options.label: Full-body sessions give every muscle less stimulus in total, so total weekly volume is effectively lower
Spreading the same weekly volume over more sessions lowers the sets per session and the fatigue within each one
Upper/lower plans prevent soreness completely, so recovery between sessions stops being a factor
Training more days a week makes each muscle grow faster because growth only happens during sessions

rubric: With equal weekly volume, higher frequency means fewer sets per session, which lowers fatigue and can keep set quality higher.
Other options claim growth happens during sessions, that volume differs, or that soreness is eliminated, all of which are wrong.

items.prompt: On sets of 10 deadlifts, a lifter's lower back stays flat through rep 6, then rounds noticeably on reps 7 to 10. Sets of 5 at the same load look clean. What does this pattern most directly indicate?

options.label: The lifter's technique is simply wrong from the start and needs a completely different pulling style
Fatigue of the trunk and back muscles is breaking form late in the set, so reps or set structure should change
The lifter has a mobility defect that would also show up as rounding on the first rep of every set
The load is too light to teach good positions, so heavier singles are the only way to fix form

rubric: Clean early reps and breakdown late in a long set point to fatigue-driven form loss, which can be managed with lower reps per set.
A fixed mobility or technique flaw would appear from rep one and in the sets of 5 as well.

items.prompt: A lifter's bench press stalled for six weeks. Logs show weekly bench sets rose from 9 to 22 over eight weeks, sleep fell to about 5.5 hours, and warm-up weights now feel heavy. What is the best reading of this?

options.label: Muscle memory has faded because the exercise has been repeated too often over the eight weeks
Accumulated fatigue from a rapid volume rise combined with poor sleep is masking strength, so recovery is the limiting factor
The program lacks variety, so replacing bench press with a new exercise is the only workable fix
The lifter has hit a genetic ceiling in bench press, which is shown by the length of the stall alone

rubric: Heavy warm-ups, falling sleep and a big volume jump point to recovery-limited performance rather than a true ceiling.
Genetic ceiling and variety explanations ignore the evidence in the log.

items.prompt: A lifter's squat has stalled for four weeks. Which observations point to accumulated fatigue rather than a lack of training stimulus? Select all that apply.

options.label: Training volume has been flat for six months and sessions feel easy
Resting heart rate and mood have worsened over the same weeks as the stall
Performance rebounds after several lighter days with no change to the program afterward
Reported effort on usual working weights has climbed even though the bar weight is unchanged

rubric: Rising effort at constant load, worsening resting markers and a rebound after rest all indicate fatigue masking fitness.
Flat volume with easy sessions suggests too little stimulus, which is the opposite diagnosis.

items.prompt: A lifter squatting 3 days a week adds leg press and walking lunges to the program. Total weekly leg sets jump from 10 to 24 in one week. Ten days later she has knee pain on stairs, and her squat form is unchanged. She asks what most likely caused the pain. Which analysis fits the evidence best?

options.label: Her form must have changed unnoticed, because pain only arises from technique faults
The lunges are always unsafe, so any lifter who adds them will be injured at once
The abrupt jump in leg volume exceeded what her tissues had adapted to, so load rose faster than capacity
The squat itself is inherently harmful to knees, so the pain would have appeared without the new exercises

rubric: The timing after a 140% volume increase points to load outpacing tissue adaptation, which is a progression error.
Distractors blame the squat, the lunge or hidden technique faults and ignore the sudden jump in volume.

items.prompt: An intermediate lifter wants steady squat progress and can only add small increments. Criteria: sustainable over months, low risk of grinding failed reps, and clear signals for when to add weight. Which progression scheme best meets them?

options.label: Training to failure on every set each session and choosing the load by feel on that day
Double progression: work in a rep range such as 6 to 8 and add weight once every set reaches the top
Switching exercises every two weeks to keep the muscles guessing so progress never stops
Adding 5 kg to the bar every session until a rep fails, then repeating the same load for weeks

rubric: Double progression gives a clear rule for adding weight and keeps reps controlled, so it suits the stated criteria for an intermediate.
Session-to-session jumps suit beginners, while constant failure and exercise rotation give poor signals and recovery.

items.prompt: A coach reviews a plan for a lifter whose goal is muscle size: six days a week of full-body sessions, each built around heavy singles at 95%+ of maximum, with little other work. What is the strongest criticism of the plan?

options.label: Singles cannot build any strength at all, so the plan fails even on its own terms
Its heavy singles give little volume for growth and heavy fatigue for the time spent, so it fits the goal poorly
Training six days a week is impossible to recover from for anyone, whatever the intensity
The plan needs lighter weights for every set because heavy loads never stimulate muscle

rubric: For hypertrophy, weekly volume matters; maximal singles carry high neural fatigue and few productive sets, so the plan mismatches the goal.
The other critiques overstate: frequency alone is not the issue, singles do build strength, and heavy loads can stimulate muscle.

items.prompt: A lifter has 3 days a week and 45 minutes per session. Criteria: improve squat, bench and deadlift, keep each lift trained at least twice a week at manageable fatigue, and limit session length. Which plan is best?

options.label: Three sessions of all three lifts at near-maximal effort, with no variation in intensity across the week
A body-part split with chest, back and legs on separate days, using isolation exercises only
Three full-body sessions, each with one main lift and one or two lighter variations, rotating which lift is heaviest
One lift per day, trained once a week with high volume, leaving the other two lifts idle that week

rubric: Rotating heavy and light exposures gives twice-weekly practice of each lift within the time limit and keeps fatigue manageable.
Once-a-week lifts, daily maximal work and isolation-only splits each break one stated criterion.

items.prompt: A lifter has trained hard for seven weeks. Performance is flat, soreness lingers and motivation is low, but he has no pain or illness. Criteria: protect long-term progress, avoid losing much fitness, and keep the plan going. Which choice is best?

options.label: Stop training for two months so that all fatigue is cleared before any further work
Switch to a new program with entirely new lifts immediately to restore motivation
Schedule a planned deload week with reduced volume at similar exercises, then resume progression
Add extra sets and extra days to force the body past the stall through sheer effort

rubric: A short deload dissipates fatigue while preserving skill and fitness, matching all three criteria.
Long breaks lose fitness, extra work worsens fatigue, and an entire program change discards a plan that may be sound.

items.prompt: A lifter with shoulder pain at the top of the barbell overhead press wants to keep building shoulders and triceps. Criteria: keep pressing strength work, avoid the painful range, and keep progressive overload measurable. Which option is the best trade-off?

options.label: Remove all pressing and train only legs until the pain disappears entirely
Swap to a landmine or incline press in a pain-free range and track load and reps as before
Switch to very high-rep light lateral raises only and stop recording loads and reps
Continue the barbell overhead press and push through the pain because it will fade as the shoulder adapts

rubric: A pain-free pressing variation keeps the stimulus and measurable overload while avoiding the aggravating range.
Other options either ignore pain, drop all pressing, or give up trackable progression.

items.prompt: A coach is deciding between fixed percentages of a one-rep max and RPE-based autoregulation for an intermediate lifter whose sleep and stress vary a lot. Which are sound reasons to favour RPE-based loading? Select all that apply.

options.label: It removes the need for any record keeping, because effort alone guides every decision
It keeps working sets at a consistent proximity to failure even when daily strength fluctuates
It adjusts the day's load to the lifter's actual readiness instead of a number set weeks earlier
It depends on the lifter's ability to judge effort, which can be learned with practice

rubric: RPE scales the load to daily readiness and keeps effort consistent, which suits a lifter with variable sleep and stress.
RPE still needs records, and the skill requirement is a limitation to manage rather than a reason to choose it.

items.prompt: A lifter has 8 weeks before a powerlifting meet. Criteria: peak maximal strength on meet day, keep technique sharp on the competition lifts, and arrive fresh. He is deciding among four plans. Which is best?

options.label: Raise both volume and intensity until the final day, so the body is pushed as hard as possible
Replace the competition lifts with unrelated variations so that they are not tired when the meet comes
Gradually raise intensity on the competition lifts while cutting volume, with a lighter final week before the meet
Keep volume at its current high level and test a new maximum single every week through to the meet

rubric: Raising intensity while reducing volume, with a taper, peaks strength while keeping skill and freshness.
The other plans leave fatigue high, drop specificity, or never allow recovery before the meet.

items.prompt: A coach claims every hypertrophy set must go to complete muscular failure or it is wasted. Judged against the criteria of growth per unit of fatigue and sustainable weekly volume, which critique is strongest?

options.label: Failure is required because only the last grinding rep recruits high-threshold fibers, so stopping short wastes the set
Failure should be avoided entirely because it causes damage that blocks growth, so every set should end with 5+ reps left
Failure matters only for heavy singles, so higher-rep sets should stop at a fixed rep count regardless of effort
Sets stopped 1–3 reps short of failure give similar growth with less fatigue, so more weekly volume stays recoverable

rubric: Sets near failure stimulate similar growth, and leaving a few reps in reserve limits fatigue so more productive volume fits in recovery.
Distractors reflect the all-or-nothing beliefs that failure is mandatory or harmful.

items.prompt: A shift worker's sleep varies from 4 to 9 hours between sessions. The program must keep overload progressing, avoid junk fatigue on bad days, and stay simple to log. Which loading method best fits these criteria?

options.label: Lifting only when fully rested and skipping sessions after poor sleep, because fatigued training always blunts adaptation
Maximal singles each session to measure readiness, then setting the other work from how fast that single moves
Fixed percentages of a tested max every session, because predetermined loads remove bias and guarantee steady overload
Working sets set by an RPE target with a percentage-based top set as anchor, so load flexes with readiness while progress stays trackable

rubric: RPE-based autoregulation anchored to a reference lets load adjust to daily state while still logging progression.
Rigid percentages ignore readiness, skipping sessions stalls progress, and daily maxes add fatigue.

items.prompt: After six weeks of rising volume, an intermediate lifter has stalled lifts, achy joints and poor sleep. Judged on restoring recovery while keeping strength and technique, which response is best?

options.label: Add a week of extra lighter volume to build work capacity, since fatigue means conditioning is the limiting factor
Keep loads close to recent weights but halve the sets for a week, so fatigue drops while strength and technique are retained
Take a full week away from the gym, since only complete rest clears accumulated fatigue and restores the joints
Switch immediately to a new program with all new exercises, since the stall proves the old movements stopped working

rubric: A volume-reduced deload with maintained intensity dissipates fatigue while preserving skill and strength.
Distractors overcorrect with total rest, add more load, or misattribute the stall to exercise choice.

items.prompt: A powerlifter meets the competition in three weeks. Judged against arriving fresh with confident, practiced heavy loads, which peaking plan is best?

options.label: Max out on all three lifts the week before the meet to confirm numbers, since testing builds neural readiness and confidence
Drop all loads to about 60% for three weeks, since lighter weights let the body fully supercompensate by meet day
Cut volume sharply but keep a few heavy sets near competition weights, so fatigue clears without losing practice at intensity
Keep volume high until meet week to maximise fitness, then rest only the final two days before competition

rubric: A taper reduces volume while maintaining heavy exposure, so fatigue falls without detraining or losing skill at heavy loads.
Distractors either add fatigue (maxing, high volume) or remove intensity entirely.

items.prompt: A lifter's bench stalls, with the bar slowing just off the chest while lockout is fast. They propose adding 10 weekly sets of triceps isolation work. Which critique is most accurate?

options.label: The plan is flawed only because 10 sets is too few, since triceps need at least 20 weekly sets to show any effect
The plan is flawed because sticking points are purely technical, so no accessory work of any kind can help a stall
The plan targets the wrong weak point: slowing off the chest implicates chest, shoulders and bottom-position strength, and the extra sets add fatigue
The plan is sound, since triceps are the main pressing muscle and extra volume for any bench muscle always improves the lift

rubric: Accessory work should match the sticking point; a bottom-range weakness points away from triceps isolation.
Distractors assume any accessory helps, that more volume is the fix, or that accessories never matter.

items.prompt: A basketball player who will never compete in powerlifting is choosing between the conventional deadlift and the trap bar deadlift for general strength and jump power. Which judgments favor the trap bar? Select all that apply.

options.label: Greater knee travel loads the quads more, resembling the jumping pattern
It is legal in powerlifting meets, so training with it improves competition specificity
The neutral grip and more upright torso lower lumbar demand and suit limited hip mobility
Its bar path far from the body builds more lat and upper-back strength than conventional pulls

rubric: Trap bar posture reduces back demand and shifts work toward the quads, matching jump mechanics.
It is not a legal meet lift and does not build more lat strength.

items.prompt: A 45-year-old lifter feels sharp shoulder pain at the bottom of the barbell bench press but none overhead or on rows. They want to keep building pressing strength. Judged on continuing training while letting irritation settle, which approach is best?

options.label: Stop all pressing for eight weeks and only stretch, so the joint is fully unloaded and heals before any load returns
Push through with lighter loads, since tolerating discomfort desensitises the shoulder and strength carries over regardless
Keep barbell bench but add a heavier warm-up, since pain at the bottom is a sign of cold tissue rather than the movement
Swap to neutral-grip dumbbell or floor press in a pain-free range, keep pressing volume, and track symptoms while irritation settles

rubric: Modifying the painful range or grip keeps stimulus while avoiding the provoking position.
Distractors recommend complete rest, ignoring the cause, or pushing through pain.

items.prompt: A lifter trains 3 days a week for 60 minutes, wants stronger and bigger legs, and gets knee pain in deep flexion but not above parallel. Which design meets every constraint?

options.label: Daily bodyweight squats to depth for tissue tolerance, with no heavy leg work until the pain is completely gone
Only leg extensions and leg curls to avoid loaded knee flexion, kept under 60 minutes by using high reps
Full-depth front squats twice weekly to strengthen the knee through its whole range, pushing through the pain as it adapts
Box squats to parallel or leg press in a pain-free range, Romanian deadlifts and split-stance work, progressed by load within 60 minutes

rubric: It keeps heavy, progressive leg loading inside the pain-free range and fits the time limit.
Distractors ignore pain, remove heavy loading, or defer training entirely.

items.prompt: Design a simple progression for an intermediate lifter on a curl-style accessory lift. The constraints are an 8–12 rep range, sets ending 1–2 reps from failure, and an explicit rule for when load increases. Which scheme fits?

options.label: Increase reps each week without ever changing the load, since reps alone drive overload indefinitely
Add reps weekly across 3 sets of 8–12; once all sets reach 12, raise load about 2.5–5% and restart near 8
Add 5 kg every session on every lift regardless of reps, and deload only when a set is missed
Change the exercise every two weeks and hold loads constant, since novelty drives growth while fresh technique avoids injury

rubric: Double progression gives a clear rule: reps within a range, then load increases when the top is reached.
Distractors ignore rep ranges, drop the load rule, or replace progression with variety.

items.prompt: A lifter returning after 10 weeks off proposes four sessions a week with the exact weights and volume they used before the layoff. What is this design most missing?

options.label: A reduced-volume re-entry phase with load rebuilt over weeks, since tendon and work tolerance lag remembered strength
More exercise variety, since muscle memory only returns through movements the body has not seen before
A full week of rest between each session, since tendons and muscle need seven days after a long layoff
Maximal testing in week one to reset percentages, since old numbers are invalid after any layoff

rubric: Strength returns faster than connective tissue and work capacity, so a ramp-up phase is needed.
Distractors prescribe maxing, novelty, or excessive rest instead of a graded return.

items.prompt: A 58-year-old with slower recovery can train only twice weekly for 45 minutes and wants to get stronger in squat, hinge, press and pull patterns. Which plan meets all constraints?

options.label: A body-part split with chest and arms Monday and legs Thursday, six exercises each, to hit every muscle weekly
Two sessions ending with five all-out sets to failure on each main lift, to compensate for low frequency
Two full-body sessions, each with a squat or hinge, a press and a pull, one heavier and one moderate, 2–3 sets each with reps in reserve
Two sessions of only squat, bench and deadlift at 90%+ of max, since fewer exercises mean less fatigue

rubric: Full-body sessions cover all patterns at adequate frequency, with moderate volume that respects recovery.
Distractors cut frequency per pattern, overload fatigue, or use unsustainable intensity.

items.prompt: A lifter's bench rises fast off the chest but stalls near lockout. Design the program change that addresses this while keeping the competition bench in the plan.

options.label: Replace bench with deficit push-ups for six weeks, since extended range automatically fixes the top position
Add close-grip bench, pin or board presses and triceps work twice weekly, in place of some flat volume
Add wide-grip pause bench and chest flyes twice weekly, since lockout fails when the chest is under-trained
Drop bench to once a week and add only rowing, since lockout depends mainly on back strength

rubric: Lockout weakness calls for overload in the top range and triceps, substituting some flat volume.
Distractors target the chest or reduce pressing, missing the actual weak range.

items.prompt: You are building a 12-week hypertrophy block for an intermediate lifter training 4 days a week. Constraints: progress must be measurable, fatigue must stay manageable, and each muscle needs enough weekly stimulus. Which elements belong in the design? Select all that apply.

options.label: Every set taken to complete failure to maximise stimulus
A planned reduced-volume week every 4–6 weeks or when fatigue accumulates
Each muscle trained about twice weekly with roughly 10–20 hard sets
A logged load or rep progression target for each main exercise
Replacing every exercise weekly to prevent adaptation

rubric: Adequate frequency and volume, tracked progression and planned fatigue management meet the stated constraints.
Constant failure and weekly exercise churn undermine recovery and measurable progress.

items.prompt: A team-sport athlete is in season with games on Saturday. They can fit two 40-minute lifting sessions, Monday and Wednesday, and must avoid heavy soreness by Thursday. Which plan meets all of these constraints?

options.label: Monday: one heavy low-volume squat or hinge and a press, Wednesday: reduced moderate-load work with a pull, no failure or new exercises
Monday and Wednesday: high-volume body-part splits to failure, to build size while the schedule allows
Monday: max-effort singles on every lift, Wednesday: repeat them, since heavy low reps cause little soreness
Skip lifting in season entirely and put the time into extra conditioning, since strength cannot be maintained during competition

rubric: Low-volume heavy and moderate work maintains strength while limiting soreness, using familiar exercises near games.
Distractors ignore recovery, rely on repeated maxes, or abandon strength maintenance.
